transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you. I suppose I'm here because... well, it’s this scar on my wrist. I know it's probably not as bad as it looks to me, but it's just been bothering me so much lately. 

I actually got it a little while ago when I was organizing some heavy binders at work. I do bookkeeping and auditing for a small firm, and you wouldn't believe the absolute mess some of these clients bring in. Just last week, a man brought in a literal grocery bag full of crumpled receipts from 2021! I spent three hours just flattening them out on my desk. I swear, people think accountants are magicians. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, my wrist. It's just that when I’m out doing things, like at church on Sundays or when I'm playing bridge with my friends, I keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to the scar. It just feels like it’s the very first thing they notice about me now, instead of... well, me.
Has your concern about the scar been affecting your ability to enjoy or participate in your daily activities?

Well, yes, I suppose it has. I mean, I've actually been late turning in some of my bookkeeping work recently, which is very unlike me. And I've even skipped a few of my choir practices and the theater volunteering. 

We're doing The Music Man this spring at the community theater, which is just wonderful. I usually help with the props and the ushering. Last year we did Oklahoma! and you wouldn't believe the trouble we had finding a real butter churn. I drove all the way to a flea market two towns over just to find one that looked authentic! The director, Susan, is an absolute perfectionist, bless her heart, but she really pushed us on that set design. She even wanted real corn stalks, but I told her that was just asking for mice in the auditorium. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, missing things. Yes, I've skipped some of those commitments lately because I just get so caught up at home trying to make sure my wrist won't be noticed. I'll try on five different long-sleeve blouses or mess with different watches and bracelets for an hour, and by the time I feel okay about it, I'm already late for work or I just feel so flustered that I give up on going to choir altogether.
Have you been avoiding social interactions or feeling like you're pulling back from friends and family because of your concerns about the scar?

Well, I suppose I haven't really been pulling away from my friends and family, no. Not completely avoiding them, anyway. I still talk to my sister on the phone every Sunday evening. She lives down in Florida now, near Sarasota. She moved there about three years ago because her husband, Frank, has that terrible arthritis, and they thought the warm weather would help. Which it has, mostly, though Frank still complains about the humidity. He says it makes his hair frizz, which is hilarious because the man has been bald since he was forty-five! I visited them last February, and we went to this wonderful little seafood place right on the water. They had the most amazing crab cakes... 

But, oh, I'm sorry, I'm rambling again. No, I wouldn't say I'm avoiding people entirely. It's just... well, it's just harder to get out the door sometimes with all the fussing over my sleeves. But once I'm there, I'm still talking to everyone.
How would you describe the level of distress you feel when you think about the scar being noticed by others?

Well, distress... I'm not really sure how to describe the exact level of it. It's just upsetting, you know, thinking about people staring at it. It reminds me of my hairdresser, Betty. I've been going to her for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. Her salon is right next to that wonderful little bakery on Elm Street, the one that makes those incredible lemon tarts. Anyway, Betty notices absolutely everything. Just last month she noticed I had switched my shampoo, can you believe that? 

And don't even get me started on the time I tried to touch up my own roots during the pandemic. Oh, what an absolute disaster that was! It turned out this awful shade of brassy orange, like a rusty penny. I had to wear a silk scarf tied over my head for three weeks until she was allowed to open up and fix it. I looked like one of those old Hollywood actresses riding in a convertible, except I was just driving my Honda Civic to the pharmacy to pick up my vitamins. 

But... oh dear, I've lost the thread again, haven't I? I'm so sorry. You asked about the distress. I guess I just don't really know how to put a specific word or a rating to it. It just makes me feel very self-conscious and flustered, knowing it's right out there in the open.
Have you noticed any impact on your work performance or relationships due to your concerns about the scar?

Well, as far as my relationships go, I wouldn't say there's been an impact, really. I mean, my friends are used to me being a bit... particular about my clothes. Like my friend Carol. We've known each other since our girls were in Girl Scouts together. Oh, the cookies! Do you remember when they used to sell those lemon coolers? They were dusted in powdered sugar and just melted in your mouth. Now they just have the lemonades, which are fine, but it's just not the same. I used to buy five boxes of the coolers and hide them in the chest freezer so my husband wouldn't eat them all in one sitting. 

He was terrible about sweets, my husband. He could polish off half a pecan pie before I even had the coffee brewed. I remember one Thanksgiving, he actually dropped a dollop of whipped cream right on the good lace tablecloth—the one my mother brought over from Ireland. I thought I'd never get the stain out, but a little club soda and some gentle dabbing did the trick. 

Oh, but I'm getting carried away again. Work performance... well, I suppose I did mention I was late turning in some of my bookkeeping recently. But other than that, no, I haven't really noticed any big changes at work or with my friends. Just the being late part, because of the sleeves.
Are you finding it harder to concentrate on your bookkeeping work because of your concerns about the scar?

Well, yes, I suppose it has made it a bit harder to concentrate. Like I mentioned, I’ve been late turning in some of my bookkeeping work recently, which isn't like me at all. I usually pride myself on being so punctual with the ledgers. And it's not just work, actually. I’ve even skipped a few of my choir practices and my volunteer shifts at the community theater. 

The theater is putting on *The Music Man* this spring, which is just such a delight. I helped with the costumes the last time they did it, oh, it must have been a decade ago. We had the hardest time finding the right shade of red for the band uniforms. We ended up having to dye the fabric ourselves in the giant sinks in the high school cafeteria. My hands were stained pink for a week! I looked like I'd been eating cotton candy non-stop. The choir director, Mr. Henderson—he’s such a dear, though he can be a bit strict about the altos staying on pitch—he even asked if I was feeling alright because my hands looked so flushed. 

But, oh, where was I? Right, concentrating. Yes, I've skipped those commitments because I just get so caught up trying to make sure my wrist won’t be noticed. I spend so much time fussing with my cuffs and worrying about it that before I know it, I'm running late or I just decide it's easier to stay home. So, yes, I suppose it is affecting my concentration.
Do you feel like your worries about the scar are interfering with your ability to enjoy things you normally like to do?

Well, yes, I suppose it is interfering. Like I was saying, I've been late with my bookkeeping, and I've skipped choir and the theater. It just takes the joy out of it when I'm so worried about my wrist showing. I get so caught up in trying to hide it, making sure my sleeves are just right... I have this one sweater, a lovely cardigan I bought at Macy's during their white sale. It's a beautiful periwinkle blue, which brings out my eyes, or so my daughter tells me. She has the same color eyes, you know. She just had a baby, my first grandchild! A little boy named Thomas. We call him Tommy. He's just the sweetest thing, but he spits up constantly. My daughter goes through burp cloths like you wouldn't believe. I told her to try those muslin ones, they're so much softer on a baby's skin. 

Oh, goodness, listen to me. I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Enjoying things, right. Yes, it's just hard to enjoy the choir or the theater when I'm constantly pulling at my sleeves and making sure nobody can see my wrist. It's just exhausting, really.
Do you think it's possible that people might not notice your scar as much as you think they do?

Well, I suppose... I mean, deep down, I know the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me. I do try to tell myself that. But when I’m at church, or when I'm sitting down for bridge, I just keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it. Especially at bridge, because your hands are right there on the table holding the cards. 

We play every Tuesday at Martha's house. Martha makes the most wonderful iced tea, she puts a little sprig of fresh mint in it. She grows the mint right on her back patio in these beautiful terracotta pots she got on a trip to Mexico. Oh, you should have seen the pictures from that trip. She and her husband went to Cabo, I think it was? Or maybe Cancun. They stayed at an all-inclusive resort and she said the breakfast buffet was just out of this world. They had a whole station just for fresh fruit. I love a good melon, don't you? Cantaloupe is my absolute favorite, especially with a little sprinkle of salt. My mother used to salt her cantaloupe, and her watermelon, too... 

Oh, goodness, I'm rambling again. I'm so sorry. What were we saying? Right, the scar. Yes, even if they aren't actually looking, it just feels like it’s the very first thing they notice about me now when I reach for a trick or pass the collection plate.
Have you been feeling this self-conscious about your scar since you first got it, or has it gotten worse over time?

Well, I'm not really sure if it's gotten worse, exactly. It's just... it's always there on my mind since it happened. I remember the day I got the scar so clearly. It was a Tuesday, because I was baking my famous lemon pound cake for the church bake sale. I always make two—one for the sale and one for the house, because my husband, God rest his soul, he just couldn't resist a slice with his evening coffee. He used to say my pound cake was lighter than a cloud. 

Anyway, I was pulling the pan out of the oven, and I didn't realize the oven mitt had a little thin spot right near the wrist. It was one of those lovely quilted ones with the roosters on it. I bought a whole set of them at a craft fair up in Vermont years ago. The leaves were just turning, oh, it was breathtaking. We stayed at this quaint little bed and breakfast where they served fresh maple syrup... 

But, oh, I'm sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? The scar. Right. I suppose I've just been self-conscious about it from the very beginning. I haven't really noticed it getting worse, it's just a constant worry.
Do you feel like your worries about the scar are significantly affecting your overall quality of life?

Well, yes, I suppose it really is. Like I was saying a little bit ago, it's definitely taking a toll on my day-to-day. Falling behind on my bookkeeping work... which just bothers me to no end because I've always prided myself on being so punctual with my ledgers. My father was an accountant, actually. He had this magnificent antique adding machine on his desk. Oh, it was heavy, solid metal with those lovely round glass keys. I used to sit on his lap and press them down when I was a little girl. He always smelled like Old Spice and peppermint. He kept a little tin of peppermint pastilles in his breast pocket. The tin had a picture of a snowy mountain on it... I haven't seen those in years. I wonder if they still make them? I should look at the pharmacy next time I go down there. They have a wonderful new pharmacist, such a polite young man. He always asks about my grandson...

Oh, my goodness, I'm so sorry. My mind just wanders right off! You were asking about my quality of life. Yes, it's just like I mentioned earlier. Skipping out on my volunteer commitments with the choir and the theater, and being late turning in my work... it really does affect my life. I just get so tied up in knots trying to make sure the wrist won't be noticed by anyone, I end up missing out on the things I used to just do without a second thought.
Do you think it's possible that your scar is not as noticeable to others as it is to you?

Well, I... I suppose we already talked about that, didn't we? I mean, deep down I know it might not be as bad as it looks to me. I try to remind myself of that. But it's just so hard when I'm out in public. Like at the grocery store. I go to the Piggly Wiggly on Main Street. They have the best produce section. The manager, Mr. Henderson, he always makes sure the apples are polished so nicely. He’s been working there since my kids were little. Oh, my youngest, Sarah, she used to love the Red Delicious apples. She'd eat them right down to the core. Now she lives in Seattle and says she only buys organic Honeycrisp. Seattle is so rainy, though. I don't know how she stands it. She sent me a beautiful raincoat for Christmas, bright yellow with a lovely plaid lining. It reminds me of Paddington Bear. Did you ever read those books? The little bear with his marmalade sandwiches... 

Oh, dear, I'm doing it again. I am so sorry, doctor. My mind is just a sieve today. But yes, to answer your question, I do think it's possible people don't notice it as much as I do. It just doesn't feel that way when I'm out and about.
Do you find yourself thinking about the scar at the same times every day or is it more sporadic?

Well, it's... it's pretty much all the time, honestly. Not just specific times of day. Like I said before, I know the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me, but... well, when I’m at church or playing bridge with the girls, I just keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it. Like it’s the first thing they notice about me now. 

We play bridge every Thursday afternoon at Eleanor's house. She has this gorgeous sunroom that looks out over her garden. She grows the most spectacular hydrangeas. Huge, blue blooms. She says the secret is putting coffee grounds in the soil, which I always mean to try, but I drink decaf now because of my heartburn, and I'm never quite sure if decaf grounds work the same way. The doctor told me to cut back on acidic foods, which is a shame because I do love a good tomato sandwich in the summer. Just white bread, mayonnaise, a thick slice of a beefsteak tomato, and a little salt and pepper. My grandmother used to make them for us when we'd visit her down in Georgia...

Oh, goodness gracious. I've completely lost the thread again, haven't I? I'm so sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, thinking about the scar. Yes, it's just... it's constantly on my mind, especially when I'm around other people, no matter what time of day it is.
Has your concern about the scar changed in intensity over time, or has it remained fairly constant?

Well, it's... I'd say it's gotten worse, really. When I first got the scar, I thought it would just fade away, you know? Like when you scrape your knee as a child. I was always scraping my knees. We had this big oak tree in the front yard and my brother Thomas and I would climb it for hours. He was a regular monkey, that boy. He actually joined the Navy later on, spent twenty years on submarines. I can't even imagine being cooped up in a metal tube underwater for months on end. I get claustrophobic just riding the elevator at the dentist's office. Dr. Miller is on the fourth floor, and the elevator always makes this dreadful clanking sound right around the second floor... 

Oh, dear me. I've wandered off again. I am so sorry, doctor. You were asking if it's changed. Yes, it's definitely gotten more intense. At first I just wore long sleeves, but now it feels like I can't stop thinking about it, no matter what I do.
Is your concern about the scar more about how it looks to you or about what others might think of it?

Well, it's... I suppose it's really about both, but mostly it's what other people think. Like I said before, deep down I know the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me in the mirror. But when I'm out, like when I'm at church or playing bridge with the girls, I just keep feeling like everyone's eyes go right to it. Like it's the first thing they notice about me now. 

And church has been so different lately anyway. We got a new choir director, Mr. Davies. He's very enthusiastic, but he insists on doing all these modern hymns with guitars and tambourines. I miss the old organ music. Our old organist, Mrs. Gable, she played for forty years. She had the most beautiful hands, always wore these lovely pearl rings. She moved to Florida last year to be closer to her daughter. Tampa, I think. Or maybe Clearwater? I know it's on the Gulf side because she said the sunsets over the water are just spectacular. I've never been to Florida myself. The humidity just wreaks havoc on my hair. Even when I use that special anti-frizz serum my hairdresser recommended...

Oh, for heaven's sake. I'm doing it again. I am so sorry, doctor. My brain is just skipping like a scratched record. But yes, to answer you, it's mostly about other people. I just can't shake the feeling that they're staring right at it.
Do you think your scar makes you feel unattractive or does it affect how you see your body?

Well, it's... I don't know if it makes me feel completely unattractive overall, but it certainly ruins my arms. I just feel like it's this glaring flaw. It's like when you get a stain on a brand-new blouse. I had this beautiful silk blouse once, a lovely sort of peach color. I bought it for my nephew's wedding. He married a girl from Ohio, very sweet, but they had an outdoor reception in July. July! It was sweltering. And they served these little meatballs in a sort of cranberry glaze. Delicious, but one rolled right off my little appetizer plate and hit the silk. I tried club soda, I tried taking it to the dry cleaner on Main Street—Mr. Chen, he's a wizard usually, he got a terrible coffee stain out of my winter coat two years ago. But that cranberry glaze just wouldn't budge. I ended up having to give the blouse to Goodwill. I always wonder if someone bought it and just wore a sweater over it to hide the spot...

Oh, dear. I'm so sorry, doctor. I'm rambling about meatballs now. What did you ask me? Oh, about feeling unattractive. I don't think it changes how I see my whole body, really. It's just... I just hate looking at my arm now because it's ruined by that spot.
Do you feel like the scar affects how you see yourself as a whole person?

Well, no, I don't think so. I mean, I'm still the same person on the inside. I'm still just me, you know? I've been doing bookkeeping for over forty years, and that hasn't changed. I actually started back when we used those big green paper ledgers. Oh, the smell of that paper! My old boss, Mr. Henderson, he was such a stickler for neat handwriting. He used to say a messy ledger meant a messy mind. He drove this enormous Cadillac, bright yellow. It looked exactly like a giant banana coming down the street. His wife, Barbara, she used to bring us lemon bars every single Friday. I can still taste them, honestly. She used real lemon zest, not that artificial extract you get at the grocery store now. I tried to make them once for a bake sale, but the phone rang and I left them in the oven too long. It was one of those telemarketers. They always call right when you're in the middle of something important, don't they? Trying to sell extended car warranties or whatever it is... 

Oh, dear heavens, listen to me. I'm going on about lemon bars and telemarketers now. I really am sorry, doctor, my mind just wanders off down the street. But no, to answer your question, I don't think the scar changes who I am as a whole person. It's just... well, it's just that one spot on my arm that I can't stand.
Is your concern about the scar mainly about how it looks on your wrist or is it more about how it affects your overall appearance?

Well, it's really just about the wrist, I suppose. I don't think it ruins my whole appearance, just that one area. It's like... well, it's like having a beautiful garden, but there's this one stubborn weed right in the middle of the petunias. I love petunias, especially the purple ones. I tried growing them in a window box last spring, but the squirrels kept digging them up. I don't know what it is about squirrels in this neighborhood, they are just relentless. My neighbor, Arthur, he put out cayenne pepper to keep them away. He swears by it. He also has this intricate bird feeder system, on these tall poles with baffles, you know, to stop them from climbing up. But I saw one squirrel practically do gymnastics, swinging from a tree branch just to get to the sunflower seeds. They're so clever, really. Sometimes I just sit by the window with my morning coffee and watch them for hours. I drink decaf now, though. My doctor told me the caffeine was making my heart race... 

Oh, goodness me. I've done it again. I am so sorry, doctor. I'm talking about squirrels and bird feeders. But yes, to answer your question, it's mainly just the scar on my wrist that bothers me, not my overall appearance.
Is your worry about the scar more about how it looks or about how others might react to it?

Well, I suppose it's both, really. I mean, I know in my head that the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me in the mirror. But when I'm out, it just feels so... obvious. Like when I'm at church, or playing bridge on Tuesdays with the girls. I just keep feeling like everyone's eyes go right to it. Like it's the very first thing they notice about me now. Bridge has gotten so competitive lately, by the way. Martha, she's my partner, she practically memorizes the cards. She wears these big, thick glasses with a chain, the kind with little faux pearls on it. Her daughter bought it for her when she went on a cruise to Alaska. They saw glaciers and whales, apparently. I've always wanted to go on a cruise, but I get terrible seasickness. Even just being on a pontoon boat on the lake makes my stomach turn. I took Dramamine once for a ferry ride to Nantucket, and I slept through the whole trip. Woke up drooling on my husband's shoulder... 

Oh, dear, I'm so sorry, doctor. I'm off on a boat to Nantucket now. What were we talking about? Oh, right, the scar. Yes, I just feel like people are staring at it, even if I know it might not be that terrible.
Is your worry about the scar more about how it looks to you or about what others might think when they see it?

Well, I think... I'm not really sure, honestly. I suppose it's a bit of both, but I really don't know how to separate the two in my mind. When I look at it, I just feel so bothered by it, and then I think about what other people must be thinking when they see it. It's like when you wear a shirt and realize later there's a stain on it. Speaking of stains, I spilled coffee down the front of my favorite white blouse just last week. It was that nice silk one I bought on sale at Macy's. They were having their big semi-annual clearance, and you know how chaotic those can be. People grabbing things off the racks left and right. I saw a woman practically wrestle another lady for a pair of discounted shoes. They were just plain black pumps, nothing special. I haven't worn heels in years, my arches just can't take it anymore. I bought these orthopedic inserts, they cost a small fortune, but they really do help when I'm standing in line at the grocery store. The lines at the Piggly Wiggly have been atrocious lately. They only ever have two registers open, and the self-checkout always yells at me about an unexpected item in the bagging area...

Oh, for heaven's sake, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I am so sorry, doctor. Groceries and shoes. I just don't know the answer to your question, really. I just know it bothers me, whether it's me looking at it or someone else.
Is your worry about the scar more about how it looks or about how it might change how people interact with you?

Well, I suppose I don't really know. I haven't noticed people treating me any differently, per se, but I still worry about it. It's like... well, it's just always there in the back of my mind. Like when you leave the house and you can't remember if you left the iron on. I did that once, years ago, when we lived in the old house on Elm Street. I was halfway to work—I was doing the books for a local hardware store back then, Mr. Henderson's place. He was such a sweet man, always gave the kids free lollipops when they came in. Anyway, I was halfway there and I just panicked. I had to turn the car around and drive all the way back. It turned out I had unplugged it, but the cord was just resting near the outlet. My husband always said I was a worrywart. He was so relaxed about everything. He could fall asleep anywhere, even sitting straight up in a chair. We bought this La-Z-Boy recliner when he retired, this ugly brown corduroy thing, but he loved it so much... 

Oh, goodness, listen to me ramble. I'm sorry, doctor. I'm off in the past again. But to your question, I really don't know if it changes how people interact with me. I just know I worry about it.
